```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 0.3)

# draws n full-width blank lines (margin to margin) for handwritten answers,
# as a single plot so spacing is deterministic; pair with fig.height = 0.3 * n
blank_lines <- function(n = 1) {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, n), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    segments(0, n - i + 0.5, 1, n - i + 0.5, lwd = 1)
  }
}

# reserves blank work space (no ruled lines) for equation manipulation /
# show-your-work; pair with fig.height set to however much room is needed
blank_space <- function() {
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot.new()
}

# keeps a prompt and its answer space on one PDF page: place `r nq(...)` on its
# own line just above the prompt. Emits nothing in non-LaTeX output. lines =
# lines of prompt text, rows = rows of blank space below it (0.3 in each),
# extra = any other height (in inches), e.g. a code block
nq <- function(lines, rows = 0, extra = 0) {
  if (!knitr::is_latex_output()) return("")
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf("\n\\needspace{%.2fin}\n", 0.23 * lines + 0.15 + 0.3 * rows + extra))
}
```

```{r key-helpers, include=FALSE}
ans_col <- rgb(200, 0, 130, maxColorValue = 255)
# redraws blank_table() so cells flagged TRUE in `ans` use the answer color
blank_table <- function(headers, body, col_widths = NULL,
                        header_height = 0.35, row_height = 0.5,
                        cex = 0.95, bold_rows = integer(0), ans = NULL) {
  nc <- length(headers); nr <- length(body)
  if (is.null(col_widths)) col_widths <- rep(1, nc)
  col_widths <- col_widths / sum(col_widths)
  cx <- c(0, cumsum(col_widths))
  h_total <- header_height + nr * row_height
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0), family = "serif")
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, h_total), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
  y <- h_total
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  y <- y - header_height
  segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = 1.5)
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    y <- y - row_height
    segments(0, y, 1, y, lwd = if (i == nr) 1.5 else 0.5,
             col = if (i == nr) "black" else "grey70")
  }
  for (v in cx) segments(v, 0, v, h_total, lwd = 1)
  yh <- h_total - header_height / 2
  for (j in seq_len(nc)) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yh, labels = headers[[j]], font = 2, cex = cex)
  y <- h_total - header_height
  for (i in seq_len(nr)) {
    yc <- y - row_height / 2
    for (j in seq_len(nc)) {
      val <- body[[i]][[j]]
      is_ans <- !is.null(ans) && isTRUE(ans[[i]][[j]])
      if (!identical(val, "")) text((cx[j] + cx[j + 1]) / 2, yc, labels = val, cex = cex,
                                    font = if (i %in% bold_rows) 2 else 1,
                                    col = if (is_ans) ans_col else "black")
    }
    y <- y - row_height
  }
}
```

```{r key-values, include=FALSE}
curv_binom <- function(k, n) n / ((k / n) * (1 - k / n))
se_3 <- 1 / sqrt(curv_binom(12, 30))
se_30 <- 1 / sqrt(curv_binom(120, 300))
wald_chytrid <- 0.1 + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(curv_binom(2, 20))
nll_chytrid <- function(p) -dbinom(2, 20, p, log = TRUE)
f_cut <- function(p) nll_chytrid(p) - nll_chytrid(0.1) - 2
range_chytrid <- c(uniroot(f_cut, c(1e-6, 0.1))$root, uniroot(f_cut, c(0.1, 0.9))$root)
```

\ans{\textbf{Answer key.} Answers are in magenta.}


**NRES 746, Week 8, Lecture 2: Curvature by Hand (optional take-home)**


**Optional practice; you don't need to turn it in.** Try Parts 1 and
2 on paper before you open a laptop. Part 3 uses R.

## Putting it in context

In Week 7 we saw that the curvature of the negative log-likelihood
(NLL) at its minimum measures how much the data tell us about a
parameter. For a parameter $\theta$ with MLE $\hat\theta$:

$$\text{SE}(\hat\theta) \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{NLL}''(\hat\theta)}}
\qquad \text{approximate 95\% interval: } \hat\theta \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$$

`optim(..., hessian = TRUE)` estimates $\text{NLL}''(\hat\theta)$
numerically. Here you find it with calculus, for two models you already
know. (Part 1 starts where the Newton's method take-home did, then goes
on to the standard error.)


## Part 1: Pika haypiles (Poisson)

The Week 7 pika data: active haypiles in six talus plots, 2, 5, 3, 0, 4,
4, modeled as Poisson with mean $\lambda$. Dropping terms that don't
involve $\lambda$,

$$\text{NLL}(\lambda) = n\lambda - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i\right)\log\lambda$$

**1a.** Find $\text{NLL}'(\lambda)$ and $\text{NLL}''(\lambda)$.

\ans{$\text{NLL}'(\lambda) = n - \dfrac{\sum y_i}{\lambda}$, \qquad $\text{NLL}''(\lambda) = \dfrac{\sum y_i}{\lambda^2}$}


**1b.** Evaluate $\text{NLL}''(\hat\lambda)$ at $\hat\lambda = 3$ for
the six plots, and again for 24 plots with the same mean (each count
appearing four times). Give the SE for each.



6 plots: $\text{NLL}''(\hat\lambda) =$ \ans{$18/9 = 2$}, SE = \ans{$1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.71$} \qquad
24 plots: $\text{NLL}''(\hat\lambda) =$ \ans{$72/9 = 8$}, SE = \ans{$1/\sqrt8 \approx 0.35$}


**1c.** Substitute $\hat\lambda = \bar{y} = \sum y_i / n$ into your
$\text{NLL}''$ and simplify to get a general formula for
$\text{SE}(\hat\lambda)$ in terms of $\hat\lambda$ and $n$. What happens
to the SE when $n$ quadruples?

\ans{$\text{NLL}''(\hat\lambda) = \dfrac{n\hat\lambda}{\hat\lambda^2} = \dfrac{n}{\hat\lambda}$, so $\text{SE}(\hat\lambda) = \sqrt{\hat\lambda/n}$. Quadrupling $n$ halves the SE.}


## Part 2: Frog detection (binomial)

In Lab 5, Act 1, you pooled three wetlands and heard the frog on $K = 12$
of $N = 30$ visits, so $\hat p = 0.4$. Dropping the binomial
coefficients,

$$\text{NLL}(p) = -K\log p - (N - K)\log(1 - p)$$

**2a.** Find $\text{NLL}''(p)$. (Watch the chain rule on $\log(1-p)$.)

\ans{$\text{NLL}'(p) = -\dfrac{K}{p} + \dfrac{N-K}{1-p}$, \qquad $\text{NLL}''(p) = \dfrac{K}{p^2} + \dfrac{N-K}{(1-p)^2}$}


**2b.** Evaluate $\text{NLL}''(\hat p)$ and the SE for your survey
($K = 12$, $N = 30$) and for your colleague's survey ($K = 120$,
$N = 300$). Check: one of your curvatures should be 125.

\ans{Curvatures: $12/0.16 + 18/0.36 = `r curv_binom(12, 30)`$ (3 wetlands) and `r curv_binom(120, 300)` (30 wetlands).}

3 wetlands: SE = \ans{$1/\sqrt{125} \approx `r round(se_3, 3)`$} \qquad 30 wetlands: SE = \ans{$1/\sqrt{1250} \approx `r round(se_30, 4)`$}


**2c.** Substitute $\hat p = K/N$ and simplify to get a general formula
for $\text{SE}(\hat p)$. Have you seen this formula before?

\ans{$\text{NLL}''(\hat p) = \dfrac{N}{\hat p(1-\hat p)}$, so $\text{SE}(\hat p) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{N}}$.}

\ans{Yes: the standard error of a proportion from intro stats.}


**2d.** The Week 7 Monday WOD (*Reading the Interval*) had 2
chytrid-positive frogs out of 20. Use your formula from 2c to build the
approximate 95% interval, $\hat p \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}$. What's wrong
with it? Compare it with the range you read off the NLL curve in that
WOD.

Interval: from \ans{`r round(wald_chytrid[1], 3)`} to \ans{`r round(wald_chytrid[2], 3)`}

\ans{The lower end is a negative prevalence, which is impossible. The NLL-curve range from that WOD (about `r round(range_chytrid[1], 2)` to `r round(range_chytrid[2], 2)`) stays positive and is lopsided toward higher values.}

`optim(..., method = "Brent", lower = 0.001, upper = 0.999, hessian = TRUE)`.
Does the Hessian match your answer to 2b?

`optim()` Hessian: \ans{about 125 (yes, it matches 2b)}
